case.title: The Silent Camera
case.hook: Last night I put one more camera, CAM 6, by the porch light at our pond. At 9:41 it filmed moths around the light. By 9:52 they were gone, and the camera saw nothing else move. But my bat detector (a microphone that records bat clicks) printed something at 9:52. And there’s a bat house across the pond.
case.question: What caught the moths in the dark, and how did it find them?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

stills.alt: Night-vision camera picture: a moth flying beside a bright porch light.
The same porch light 11 minutes later. There are no moths anywhere.
A bat detector printout. Each green mark is one click, too high for people to hear. First there are slow clicks, then faster clicks, then a fast BUZZ of clicks, then it goes quiet.
A tall wooden bat house on poles at the edge of a Florida park.

clues.t: A bat makes its own stimulus. It clicks, and the echo bouncing off a moth comes back to its ears. A quicker echo means a closer moth.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: build a strong model
clues.t: A strong pathway model has all four steps in order, arrows between them, a “signal” arrow to the brain, and a caption about a survival need.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: match the sense
clues.t: Every animal uses the same four steps. What changes is the stimulus and the sense organ that can pick it up: ears for echoes, a nose for smells.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: fix the broken models
clues.t: A model that skips a step can’t explain what the animal did. Something has to notice the stimulus, and the brain has to decide.

solve.title: What happened at the pond?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: A bird swooped in and spotted the moths by the porch light.
options.why: Check the printout and Clue 1. The detector heard clicks that sped up into a buzz. Birds don’t click like that. Bats do.

options.t: A bat from the bat house clicked. The echoes off the moths reached its ears, its brain worked out where each moth was, and it swooped. Same four steps as an eagle, with a different stimulus and sense organ.
options.why: Case cracked! The camera missed the bat because it was small, fast and dark. The detector heard everything. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

options.t: Nothing caught them. The moths just flew away.
options.why: Look at the printout again: slow clicks, faster clicks, then a BUZZ at the exact minute the moths disappeared. Something was hunting. Check Clue 1.

echo.afterText: You already know the four steps
echo.title: Echo hunt in the dark
todo: Press Click! The click bounces off a moth and comes back. That bounce is an echo.
Read the echo time (ms = thousandths of a second) and compare it with the test click.
Drag the 📍 pin to where the moth is, or tap that spot. Find the moth 3 times.

why.t: A microphone that records bat clicks. Most are too high for people to hear, so it prints a picture of each click.

echo.alt: A Florida bonneted bat’s face, with very large ears.
echo.credit: Florida bonneted bat, Shalana Gray, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0). Moth by a porch light, Fir0002, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

wall.t: Test click: the echo off the pond railing, 3 m away, came back in 17 ms.

echo.ask: Click, read the echo time, then show where the moth is.
echo.needClick: Click first, then read how long the echo took.
echo.closer: Too far. This echo came back quicker, so the moth is closer than that.
echo.farther: Too close. This echo took longer, so the moth is farther away than that.
echo.foundLine: Found it! {ms} ms means {m} m away. You just did the bat’s brain step.
echo.win: Three moths found! A bat makes its own stimulus: it clicks, and the echo comes back to its ears. Its brain uses the echo time to work out where the moth is. That’s a clue.

why.t: The Florida bonneted bat is Florida’s biggest bat, and one of the rarest. It hunts flying insects at night.

arrows.q: Arrow 1 (stimulus → sense organ): what does this arrow show?

opts.t: The echo reaching the bat’s ears

opts.miss: That’s not part of this hunt. What travels from the moth to the bat?
The moth doesn’t change. What comes back from the moth to the bat?

arrows.q: Arrow 2 (sense organ → brain): what travels on this arrow?

opts.miss: The moth stays outside the bat! Inside the body, a message travels.

opts.t: A signal (a message inside the body)

opts.miss: The sound stops at the ear. What carries the news from the ear to the brain?

arrows.q: Arrow 3 (brain → body): what does this arrow show?

opts.miss: Echoes are outside the bat. This arrow starts in the brain.
Think about the hunt. What did the brain tell the wings to do?

caption.q: Last step: add a caption about a survival need.

opts.t: This is a Florida bonneted bat.
opts.miss: That’s just a name. Which survival need does this pathway help with?

opts.t: Echoes help the bat find food in the dark.

opts.miss: True, but “cool” isn’t a survival need. Food, water, air, shelter or safety?

meter: + an arrow for what it noticed
build.win: That’s a strong pathway model: four steps in order, three arrows (one labeled signal) and a caption. That’s a clue.

compare.title: Match the sense
todo: Drag in the sense organ that can pick it up, or tap a sense organ and then a dashed box.

why.t: Each sense organ picks up one kind of stimulus. Ears pick up sound, eyes pick up light, a nose picks up smells, and feelers pick up touch.

compare.q: Look across all four models. What stayed the SAME every time?

opts.miss: Ears, eyes, a nose, feelers: those all changed.

opts.t: The four steps, in the same order

opts.miss: An echo, a fish, a smell, a shake: those all changed.

todo: Read the volunteer’s model and pick what’s wrong.

why.t: Scientists check each other’s models. If a step is missing, the model can’t explain what happened.

welcome.label: Welcome · the silent camera
welcome.script: Last night, my new camera by the pond filmed moths around the porch light. Eleven minutes later they were gone, and the camera saw nothing. But my bat detector heard plenty. Look at the printout in the case file: slow clicks, faster clicks, then a buzz. Something was hunting in the dark. Help me figure out how it found those moths.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · echo hunt (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Bats make their own stimulus. A bat clicks, and the sound bounces off a moth and comes back as an echo. The quicker the echo comes back, the closer the moth is. Try it yourself: click, read the echo time, and find the moth.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Say each word. For pathway, trace the four steps with your finger in the air.

part1.label: Part 1 · build a strong model (Clue 2)
part1.script: Here’s what makes my models strong. Four steps in order. An arrow between each one, with the word signal on the arrow to the brain. And a caption about a survival need. Build one for the bonneted bat, and watch the meter fill up.

part3.label: Part 3 · match the sense (Clue 3)
part3.script: Every animal uses the same four steps, but not the same senses. Look at what each animal notices. Then give it the sense organ that can pick that up. An echo needs ears. A smell needs a nose. When all four are done, look across the models. What stayed the same?

explore.label: Part 4 · fix the broken models (Clue 4)
explore.script: My volunteers drew models last night, and some of them are broken. A step is missing. A model that skips a step can’t explain what the animal did. Find what’s wrong, add the missing step, then press Run and watch the signal go all the way through.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: what caught the moths, and how did it find them? Then answer two questions, build two pathway models of your own, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says one model is enough to understand every animal. Hmm. Think about the bat, the eagle, the bear and the crab. Could one model explain them all? Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.script: Case closed! A Florida bonneted bat clicked, listened for the echoes, and its brain did the rest. Same four steps as an eagle, just a different sense. Next week, we’ll look at families: how Florida plants and animals pass their traits to their young.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how animals notice and respond?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A strong model shows the four steps in order, with arrows that show the signal.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “model”, “four steps”, “arrows” and “signal”. Those words carry the idea. Small words like “a” and “the” don’t.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.

items.name: Florida bonneted bat
items.t: Echoes of its own clicks bouncing off a moth → big ears → works out where the moth is → swoops and grabs the moth.

items.name: Anhinga

items.name: Florida black bear
items.t: The smell of ripe saw palmetto berries → a powerful nose → decides “food!” and which way to go → follows the smell to the berries.

items.name: Blue crab
items.t: A tiny shake in the water from something coming close → feelers (antennae) → decides “danger!” → raises its claws or scoots sideways to hide.
